content: Magnetism, in the field of physics, refers to the phenomenon where materials exert attractive or repulsive forces on other materials. Certain materials, such as nickel, iron, cobalt, and their alloys, are well-known for their easily detectable magnetic properties and are commonly referred to as magnets. However, all materials, to varying degrees, are influenced by the presence of a magnetic field. Magnetism also plays a critical role in physics as one of the two components of electromagnetic waves, such as light. History of Magnetism The earliest recorded scientific discussion of magnetism is attributed to Thales of Miletus, who lived between approximately 625 BC and 545 BC, as noted by Aristotle. In China, the first literary reference to magnetism appears in the 4th-century BC text Book of the Devil Valley Master (鬼谷子), which states, The lodestone makes iron come or it attracts it. By 20–100 AD, the attraction of a needle by a lodestone was documented in the work of Louen-heng, stating, A lodestone attracts a needle. The Chinese scientist Shen Kuo (1031–1095) was the first to describe the magnetic needle compass and its use in improving navigation accuracy by employing the astronomical concept of true north, as detailed in his Dream Pool Essays (1088 AD). By the 12th century, the Chinese were using the lodestone compass for navigation. In Europe, Alexander Neckham described the compass and its navigational use in 1187. In 1269, Peter Peregrinus authored Epistola de Magnete, the first known treatise on the properties of magnets. The relationship between electricity and magnetism began to be understood in 1819 when Hans Christian Ørsted, a professor at the University of Copenhagen, discovered that an electric current could influence a compass needle. This discovery, known as Ørsted's Experiment, marked a pivotal moment in the study of electromagnetism. Subsequent experiments by André-Marie Ampère, Carl Friedrich Gauss, Michael Faraday, and others further elucidated the connections between electricity and magnetism. James Clerk Maxwell later synthesized these findings into Maxwell's equations, unifying electricity, magnetism, and optics into the field of electromagnetism. In 1905, Albert Einstein used these laws to develop his theory of special relativity, demonstrating that electricity and magnetism are fundamentally interlinked and inseparable. Electromagnetism has since evolved into more advanced theories, including gauge theory, quantum electrodynamics, electroweak theory, and the Standard Model. Physics of Magnetism Magnets and Magnetic Materials Every electron inherently behaves as a tiny magnet due to its intrinsic magnetic dipole moment. In most materials, the electrons are randomly oriented, resulting in no net magnetic effect. However, in a bar magnet, the electrons are aligned in the same direction, creating a cooperative effect that generates a net magnetic field. Additionally, the orbital motion of electrons around the nucleus can sometimes contribute to the magnetic field, analogous to how a current-carrying loop of wire generates a magnetic field. Under certain conditions, the motion of electrons can align to produce a measurable total magnetic field. The magnetic behavior of a material depends on its structure and electron configuration. Various forms of magnetic behavior have been observed, including diamagnetism, paramagnetism, ferromagnetism, antiferromagnetism, ferrimagnetism, metamagnetism, spin glass, and superparamagnetism. Magnetism, Electricity, and Special Relativity Einstein's theory of special relativity reveals that electricity and magnetism are fundamentally interconnected. Magnetism cannot exist independently of electricity, and vice versa, due to relativistic effects such as length contraction and time dilation. When both are considered together, the resulting theory of electromagnetism is fully consistent with special relativity. For example, a phenomenon that appears purely electric to one observer may appear purely magnetic to another, depending on their frame of reference. Special relativity thus mixes electricity and magnetism into a single, inseparable phenomenon called electromagnetism, much like it unifies space and time into spacetime. An electric current or magnetic dipole generates a magnetic field, which in turn exerts magnetic forces on other particles within the field. Maxwell's equations, which simplify to the Biot-Savart law for steady currents, describe the origin and behavior of these fields. Magnetism arises whenever electrically charged particles are in motion, such as the movement of electrons in an electric current or the orbital motion of electrons around an atomic nucleus. Quantum-mechanical spin also contributes to magnetism. The force experienced by a charged particle moving through a magnetic field is given by the cross product of the particle's velocity vector and the magnetic field vector. This force is perpendicular to both the particle's motion and the magnetic field, meaning it can change the particle's direction but not its speed. The magnitude of the force depends on the angle between the velocity and magnetic field vectors. The right-hand rule is a useful tool for determining the direction of the velocity vector, magnetic field, and force. Magnetic Dipoles A common source of magnetic fields in nature is the magnetic dipole, which has a north pole and a south pole. These terms originate from the use of magnets as compasses, which interact with the Earth's magnetic field to indicate geographic north and south. Opposite poles attract, meaning the Earth's north magnetic pole is actually magnetically south. Magnetic dipoles tend to align themselves in opposition to an external magnetic field to minimize the energy stored in the field. For example, two bar magnets placed side by side will align north to south, reducing the net magnetic field. Reorienting them to point in the same direction requires energy, which is then stored in the resulting magnetic field. Magnetic Monopoles Unlike electric charges, magnetic poles cannot be isolated. Cutting a bar magnet in half results in two smaller bar magnets, each with a north and south pole. A magnetic monopole, if it exists, would be a fundamentally different type of magnetic object, acting as an isolated north or south pole. Monopoles would carry magnetic charge, analogous to electric charge. Despite extensive searches since 1931, magnetic monopoles have never been observed and may not exist. However, some theoretical physics models predict their existence. Paul Dirac proposed in 1931 that the symmetry between electricity and magnetism suggests the possibility of isolated magnetic poles. Using quantum theory, Dirac showed that the existence of magnetic monopoles could explain the quantization of electric charge. Certain grand unified theories predict monopoles as solitons, or localized energy packets, rather than elementary particles. Initial models suggested that monopoles created during the Big Bang would have been so abundant and massive that they would have halted the universe's expansion. The concept of cosmic inflation resolved this issue, allowing for the existence of monopoles while making them rare enough to align with current observations. Units of Electromagnetism SI Units Related to Magnetism Gauss (G): The CGS unit of magnetic flux density or magnetic induction (B). Oersted: The CGS unit of magnetic field strength. Maxwell: The CGS unit of magnetic flux. μ₀ (Permeability of Free Space): A constant value of (4π × 10^{-7} , text{N}/(text{ampere-turn})^2).
